Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 and under the urgent and pressing circumstances which appear in the following motion, I would move, if approval is given, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House, as the elected branch of the ultimate and highest tribunal in the country, concerned that justice should not only be done but be seen to be done, and that judicial and bureaucratic officials shall not make improper or unexpected use of laws enacted in parliament, requests that the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General inquire into and report to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on certain facts relating to the case of Peter Treu who, after being under charge and trial for approximately four years under the Official Secrets Act, behind a strict curtain of secrecy, was recently convicted and sentenced to imprisonment and, in particular, the allegation that Treu was commanded not to discuss the case even after conviction and was granted bail on appeal only on the same basis, and that the committee be required to consider the provisions of the Official Secrets Act which permit this kind of Star Chamber proceedings, with a view to recommending suitable changes.

Mr. Speaker, no, the treaty itself is not in question. With respect to this particular pipeline, we have undertaken to follow the principle of non-discrimination, particularly with respect to taxation, so that no province will tax this specific pipeline in a way different from the taxation of similar pipelines. That is the obligation that Canada has made with the United States through the transit pipeline treaty. In concluding the treaty on the pipeline with the United States, it seemed appropriate to secure assurances from the provinces that they would live up to the terms of the treaty in taxation matters.

subsubtopic: MERCURY POISONING STUDY
speechtext: Did the Department of National Health and Welfare begin its study on mercury poisoning in Canada and, if so, what will be the cost of such study and, how many persons will it employ?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MERCURY POISONING STUDY
speechtext:
The medical services branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare has, since 1971, been carrying out a program of investigation surveillance and education in areas of the country, such as northwest Ontario and northwest Quebec, known to be affected by mercury contamination of the environment. In 1976, this program was expanded to include investigations on Indian reserves in all the provinces and in all communities in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. To date, the program has involved some 24,000 tests in over 200 communities. The results of these tests are released regularly by the department. These tests are performed as part of the ongoing contaminants program of the medical services branch and mostly by employees of the branch as part of their regular duties. In certain specific areas, such as northwest Ontario and northwest Quebec, additional nursing staff and local health workers have been hired. On February 27, 1978
an agreement amongst the federal government, the department of social affairs of Quebec, the Donner Canadian Foundation and McGill University, was signed in Montreal. This provides for the carrying out by McGill University, of detailed epidemiological study on the health effects of methylmercury in northwest Quebec. The study is being funded equally by the federal and provincial governments and the Donner Canadian Foundation. Each of these parties has committed $125,000 for a total of $375,000 over a two year period. McGill University will be utilising the services of a number of its faculty during the course of the study. There will also be some short term employment of individuals in Montreal and in the communities being studied. These arrangements are being under the terms of the contract by McGill University. Information already collected by the medical services branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is being used as a basis for this study.

The House resumed, from Monday March 13, consideration of Bill C-4, to amend the Aeronautics Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and motion of Mr. Mazankowski (p. 3708).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak about the amendment to Bill C-4 presented by our transport critic, I would like to say that I strongly subscribe to the intent and the purpose of this amendment. There is a need for careful scrutiny of government regulations. There is no question that in the past, regardless of the form of legislation, the public and certainly members of parliament have shown a great deal of concern in the House and through the media about the nature of amendments, orders in council, regulations and so forth which come before us, or which we find out about after legislation has been approved.

May 12, 1978

One must ask what changes in the regulations or what new regulations will go forward to resolve problems at the community airport level. I am reminded of the circumstances surrounding the Castlegar airport, and I wonder whether regulations will put some form of stricture on that operation. The operation to date has shown signs of federal stricture. Positive decisions have been made by regional authorities, and negative decisions have been made by Ottawa-based authorities. The reverse can also happen.
Recently, after a number of years of operation at that airport, the Ministry of Transport in its benign wisdom decided that the Castlegar airport should have the benefit of a foam truck for the purpose of fighting fires. I think that is very commendable. The difficulty is that in providing a foam truck at the Castlegar airport the department did not realize that, in the freezing temperatures of winter, foam freezes. I have been applying to the Ministry of Transport now for about two years for an expansion of the facilities for the storage of equipment which services the runway. There is no storage facility in which to keep a foam truck. The only other way would be to leave other equipment sitting outside to freeze up during the winter months. I can just imagine the foam truck being called upon for immediate and urgent use in the middle of winter and it being discovered that the foam had frozen in the tanks. That would create all kinds of waves for Ottawa.
Surely in terms of regulations, and considering what will be done at the local level, there must be some form of reporting at the standing committee level, and reporting to this House. This House should have the opportunity to deny, or at least express concern about, the implementation of regulations that have an impact on flying, whether commercial or by private pilots.
Castelgar airport has an excellent record of all who use that facility. This includes the flight crews in commercial transports, private pilots, the ground crew in terms of weather and tower instructions, as well as the directors of the Selkirk College, one of the finest flying schools in Canada with some of the finest students.
On a recent visit to Selkirk College I overheard an inspector from the Ministry of Transport say what a treat it was to examine second year students at the flying school at Selkirk College. He said he did not think there was a student with a mark below 83. He stated that in Vancouver, where there are a number of flying schools, students applying for commercial licences frequently have an average of around 60 per cent, on the border line of failure. They fight with the instructors, inspectors, and examiners to try to get a pass mark. That speaks very well for the quality of students and instructors at Selkirk College.
That kind of dedication is demonstrated by students, instructors, air crew, be they private or commercial, the ground crew and those who operate at Castlegar airport. They have an outstanding record of safety, even though Castlegar airport is considered by many pilots to be one of the most awkward airports in Canada at which to land.
Aeronautics Act
There are no facilities at that airport such as VOR, a type of navigational aid that is very costly and highly sophisticated. This facility would be very useful because of the mountainous terrain and the approaches to the field. We have difficulty with transport regulations and priorities in providing some of the most essential, but in terms of sophistication almost rudimentary, navigational aids for Castlegar airport. The aid that is now there belongs in the Smithsonian Institute. Parts are difficult to obtain. I recognize the problem is supposedly going to be solved before this year is out. Hopefully it will be.
When dealing with regulations one is drawn to the concern that has emanated from the findings of the inquiry into the terrible accident at Cranbrook airport. I can only say that there, but for the grace of God, go I. It is a route I travel practically every week end. I am very disturbed by the reports that have come out in the press as a result of the coroner's inquest in Cranbrook for the past three days. It is very disturbing to hear that the ground operations at Cranbrook Airport were not aware that that ill-fated flight was going to arrive in Cranbrook ten minutes earlier.
Given the right weather conditions and passenger load, it is not unusual, particularly for a jet aircraft, to arrive at its destination five, ten or 15 minutes early. We sometimes benefit from that kind of early arrival. The passengers on that ill-fated flight reaped a different kind of benefit, though it can scarcely be called a benefit. Surely that type of incident is something that can be discussed in depth by concerned members who serve on the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is sensitive to some of these concerns. I believe also that he may be stubborn with regard to others, as is his nature. I really am dumbfounded as to how it can be concluded that it would not be possible for an aircraft to arrive at Cranbrook ten minutes early.
To remark on the other reported causes of the accident would not be appropriate for me or anyone else who lacks the experience, expertise, and knowledge to comment on them properly. They deal with the question of whether there was pilot error, mechanical error, or whatever. Much of that we will probably never know.
The Cranbrook airport has been in operation as a Ministry of Transport airport for a number of years. It enjoys a substantial amount of traffic, both private and commercial. It does not have the benefit of a tower. I might ask why Castlegar got a tower before Cranbrook. However, I would then be open to some concerns by my constituents. I am indeed pleased that a tower was constructed at Castlegar before Cranbrook, possibly because Castlegar is considered a much more difficult airport in terms of approaches. Nevertheless, the fact remains that we have our priorities mixed. There should be much greater emphasis on air traffic control.
It is incongruous that at this very moment in Castlegar the airport is under major reconstruction, with a total rebuilding of the surface. For the expenditure of a few extra dollars, there could be provision for adequate parking rather than having the

May 12, 1978
Aeronautics Act
cars parked every which way, and even out in the field. There should be provision of adequate facilities for the Castlegar airport such as for the reclaiming of baggage, especially in winter. The outdoor baggage pick-up area clearly does not demonstrate good judgment.
In Kelowna, which does not experience anything like the weather conditions at Castlegar, in fact it is positively tropical, there is indoor provision for luggage. The same is true of Cranbrook, but not so in Castlegar. They must work in cramped and confined quarters inside the terminal building, both in terms of service personnel and management as well as the representatives of PWA. The passengers are confined to a very small area. It is totally inadequate to meet the needs of the people.
There are a large number of airports in Canada. Nevertheless, the public questions the mixture of priorities in terms of the Ministry of Transport. The Minister of Transport has a habit of foisting these airport operations on to the communities. He makes it appear like a gift or a fire sale. Frequently it is the communities that end up being burned. The reaction from the communities is, "Take back your airport. We do not want the damn thing. You did not tell us the whole story". Another of the mixed reactions is, "Now that we are operating it for you, you are not prepared to spend a penny. You expect us to do all the work for you".
I am sure every municipality which has an airport is proud of that fact. They take pleasure out of being able to call their airports the City Airport of Cranbrook, the Castlegar City Airport, or the Vancouver International Airport. The communities cannot bear the load respecting airport facilities, equipment, manpower and maintenance, alone. They should not have to; they should not be asked to do that. There should be common ground and understanding before communities walk into situations such as that with their eyes blinded by the Department of Transport. At the other end of the road, there will be a big bill. Not only do local airports have cause for concern. The smaller airport facilities have cause for concern as well.
I am amazed at the Community Airport Facilities Fund. The Minister of Transport can correct me if he wants, but it is my understanding the fund per year allotted for that type of a facility is around $2 million, generally speaking. Also it is my understanding that the call on that money across Canada is in excess of $9 million. Some of these smaller community facilities-call them emergency strips, if you will-are in desperate need of upgrading in order to make them reasonably safe for private aircraft landings. Yet we have a fund of $2 million, with a demand of $9 million annually. It takes a long time for any community to reach the top of the pile. In some instances, communities find that they have been reshuffled and end up at the bottom of the pile.
The community of Kaslo made overtures to the fund for a number of years, with no results. The town of Creston was anxious to put in an airport. That town did not receive

encouragement from the Minister of Transport because it was a community with a tax base which did not allow it to make an initial start. In fact that community requires that boost and that help. As matters now stand, they will not get an airport.
Aside from the provision of facilities, buildings, plants and other structures at airports, a great deal of concern should be directed toward the question of air safety, commercial or private. After the coroner's inquest, it was revealed that there have been other instances across Canada. Apparently there was one at Dorval and, if I am not mistaken, one at North Bay or Thunder Bay. In these instances, commercial flights landed and were impeded on final approach and touchdown by vehicles on the runway such as snow removal equipment, maintenance equipment or whatever.
Surely some kind of policy or regulation to protect us from accidents of that nature is necessary. I am referring to accidents which are caused by conflicting traffic being on the runways at the same time. I think of the horrible accident which occurred in the Canary Islands a couple of years ago. In that accident I lost two good friends from Kelowna when two 747s collided on the runway. I would hate to think a remotely similar accident could occur in Canada.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has repeatedly expressed his concerns in this House for air safety. He has drawn to the attention of the minister the violations which have occurred repeatedly in the north. I am aware of a number of occasions where aircraft have crashed, resulting in the death of the crew and passengers, because of one simple failure-the failure to adhere to load limits.

speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS. ETC.
speechtext:
The responsibility for load limits rests with the commander or the pilot of the aircraft. Load limit infractions are most dangerous, a real poker game with death. They are occurring repeatedly, most particularly in the north.
I can recall making a flight in a Beaver from Smithers to Buckinghorse Lake. I had the benefit of a good pilot and a good aircraft. He wondered why the aircraft would not maintain the straight and level course which he wanted. After we landed and were unloading supplies, the pilot realized that someone back at the base in Smithers had put a drum of fuel into the back of the aircraft. He did not know it was there. The aircraft was fully loaded with equipment prior to the drum of fuel being loaded. That drum was covered up, and the pilot was not aware of it being there. It was not an easy flight for him, and it was rather uncomfortable for me. I was aware of his concerns because I am a pilot as well, but I am not as skilled as those men who fly in the north. One should not risk death by overloading. The men who fly in the north are asked repeatedly to take a chance by overloading their aircraft.
May 12, 1978

There is a host of areas which can be covered during debate on this bill. I will not attempt to cover all those areas. I thank hon. members for allowing me to continue my remarks after my time had expired. The Minister of Transport bears a tremendous responsibility in the enormous and widespread field of aviation. This responsibility is shared by his officials, who are dedicated and have proven well, but are constrained by government policy. It is difficult to comprehend that government and cabinet regulations would impinge upon the effectiveness of the Department of Transport itself or those who are under its blanket or cover.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS. ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF AIRPORTS. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity of participating in the report stage of Bill C-4 dealing with the Aeronautics Act, formerly known as Bill C-40. Members of this House are quite aware of the furor this bill caused small aircraft operators because of proposed changes in landing fees and so on. I am happy to say that because of pressures put on by those operators and other concerned groups, as well as by opposition members, we have been able to come up with some improvements to the bill during the committee process.
We now have an amendment to clause 2 which will provide for better consultation between the minister and aircraft owners and operators, and will exempt aircraft that weigh less than 5,700 kilograms from the regulation requiring a deposit of security lien for nonpayment and cases of overdue accounts.
Also during the committee process we amended clause 4 to eliminate the need to license premises used in the design of aircraft, and to provide notice by registered mail to landowners affected by zoning regulations made under the provisions of this bill. Prior to the amendment, any landowner who might be affected because of zoning changes brought in by the federal government was not even to receive the courtesy of getting a notice of that change by registered or first class mail. We managed a definite improvement there.
In addition, clause 7 was withdrawn from the bill. This would have changed licence requirements for non-scheduled air carriers.
I am happy to see that we have an amendment by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) which will permit, if 20 members of this House desire, the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications to call witnesses and report to the House concerning the proposed regulation of landing fees and other aspects of the act. We support that amendment because we feel it is important to have on-going consultations with those affected, and we want to see how this act will affect the people in its operation, and have the chance to change or negate any of its detrimental effects.
In the short time remaining to me I should like to zero in on two aspects of the bill which, in a sense, relate to the process of amendment before us and the examination of how the act operates, that is, the effects the bill will have on landowners
Aeronautics Act
because of zoning changes near airports, and the matter of air safety.
An amendment in the bill gives the federal government an opportunity to make zoning regulations in areas adjacent to airports to provide for safety in respect of commercial and private aircraft. We welcome the idea in principle that the federal Department of Transport should have some authority in zoning around airports. However, we are dismayed at the lack of provision and safeguard in the bill in the whole regulatory process to protect existing land owners from any deterimental effects of rezoning. For example, we know there is no avenue of appeal before or after publication of the regulation affecting those who are going to be rezoned. The method of determining compensation to those affected by zoning is, in the opinion of the NDP, quite inadequate. Compensation is provided only to those who are using land in a manner which does not conform to the new regulations, and the act does not compensate for injury caused by airport operations.
I think of a specific case in point which demonstrates this situation, and that is the case of the residents of the Stanley Park area near the federal airport in that community of the city of Thunder Bay. The city made a detailed representation to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, making what I thought were quite logical and proper recommendations in terms of protecting landowners adjacent to airports. They brought out a number of weaknesses in the bill which, unfortunately, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has not seen fit to address himself to by providing proper amendments.
Let me quote from this representation from the city of Thunder Bay as I think it is well worth putting on the record, and I urge the minister to take these recommendations into consideration. The city points out:
Subsection 10 only provides for compensating owners who are put in the position of contravening the zoning regulations because the use exists at the time the regulations become applicable and only on the basis of the decrease in value caused by the application balanced by any increase in value of the property which may come about by the effects of the airport. No provision is made for compensation:
(a)	where damages are attributable to disturbance of occupation or business losses;
(b)	where there are special difficulties in relocation;
(c)	in a special allowance where a residence is taken, including a fixed amount for inconvenience and the cost of finding another residence as well as an allowance for improvements to the land where the value is not reflected in the market value;
(d)	for special costs in replacing the premises;
(e)	for moving costs;
(0 for legal, survey and appraisal costs
The act does not make special provision for compensating tenants or deal separately with mortgages.
Subsection (11) limits the time for claiming compensation within two years from date of registration of the regulation. This provision without the safeguard that the owner has been properly notified would appear to assume that everyone checks his property's title every two years.
Those are the concerns of the city and property owners, and the only advance we have really made is in the area of

May 12, 1978
Aeronautics Act
notification. If there is to be a rezoning, the federal Department of Transport will send a letter to those affected. In terms of those other valid complaints we do not see any improvement. I think that is a glaring inadequacy of this bill, and unless it is overcome by regulation, or perhaps even by proper amendment, I do not see how we can support the bill as it is written. Surely property owners should not be jeopardized by "after the fact" kind of regulations, and if we have a government that believes in fairness and justice there should be a proper method of appeal, and we should have proper compensation procedures for those affected.
The other area of the bill which gives me much concern is that with reference to air safety. It is my conclusion we have a Department of Transport that is woefully negligent in this matter of air safety. I refer to that part of the country with which I am very familiar, northern Ontario, and in particular northwestern Ontario. We have seen one example after another of non-compliance with air safety regulations, nonenforcement of air safety regulations and, indeed, lax regulations in terms of air traffic in that part of the country.
The House and the public would be shocked to know that since 1970 in northern Ontario there have been more than 520 airplane accidents north of a line between Ottawa and Georgian Bay. One hundred and seventy people have died in those accidents. Between January and November, 1976, there were 57 accidents which claimed the lives of 13 people. The transport ministry official estimate states that there were almost an equal number of incidents in the same period caused by such things as fuel caps off, sliding off runways, near collisions in the air, and faulty plane maintenance. Yet the Minister of Transport likes to tell us in the House that we have one of the safest records of any country in terms of air safety.
Statistics in those specific areas indicate that we may have a very safe record when we average it out internationally, but certainly in terms of regions of Canada and the people who have to use that air travel, this is a very sad record indeed. I have called in this House for a public inquiry into the air safety aspect in northern Ontario time and time again. We have seen a department investigation in response to the clamour from the people of the area in light of these many accidents, and it was called the Slaughter and Carswell report. It brought in a devastating report on the state of air safety in northwestern Ontario.
Among many things they found overloading, falsification of log book entries, illegal and unsafe maintenance practices, flying below legal limits in bad weather, flying with insufficient flight instruments, failing to record aircraft defects, failing to train pilots although it is required by law, signing of logs by maintenance engineers without the required work being done, and employers pressuring employees into unsafe and illegal practices.
It also came to light that part of this horrendous state of the air safety situation in northwestern Ontario was that political considerations can supersede the safety of the travelling public. A memo from R. L. Bolduc, director of the ministry's

aeronautical licensing and inspection branch, indicated instances in the past where an aircraft inspector had tried to suspend the licence of an airline operating out of Red Lake, Ontario, for violating safety regulations and was told by his Ottawa superior that suspensions should never be considered until, and I quote:
-you fully consider the possibility of embarrassment to the minister and any other potential political implications-
Does embarrassment to the minister take precedence over enforcing air safety regulations? What an incredible state of affairs that we have in this country when memos such as that are given to inspectors in the field. If that alone does not justify a full public inquiry into the full operations of air traffic in northern Ontario and the whole business of the adequacy of our inspection and regulations, I do not know what does.
Despite that revelation, the number of accidents, the Slaughter and Carswell report, the minister refuses and stonewalls a full public inquiry into that situation. Instead, what the minister does is issue a press release in December of 1977 announcing that a number of recommendations, of the 15 outlined in the Slaughter and Carswell report, are being given serious consideration, and that he is hiring 12 more aviation inspectors. Well, that is commendable and we do not argue with hiring more inspectors, but that surely is not going to get to the root of the problem. It will not clear up the example I mentioned of who is telling whom when air safety regulations are to be applied or not to be applied, and under what circumstances.
Mr. Leo Bernier, the provincial minister of northern affairs, requested an inquiry because there had been 134 crashes between January and October, 1976 in which 32 people died. The Minister of Transport's office confirmed these figures but responded by saying that an inquiry was not necessary because, and I quote:
-experienced aviation specialists have been hired and positioned in our regional offices to monitor and take appropriate action to improve the standards of operation of air carriers in all parts of the country.
We have had these assurances in the past, yet we still have the incredible accident rate in this part of the country. The governament must get to the bottom of this, and the only way that can be done is by an independent inquiry or holding public hearings that will examine such things as the state of radio signals and beacons in the small airports, landing strips throughout the north, mechanical repair facilities in these small communities and, indeed, the operating procedures of the various aircraft companies themselves.
The recent developments in northern Ontario are most disconcerting, and I refer particularly to one company, Patricia Airways. Anyone who has been following the situation will be familiar with the fact that on May 12, 1977, a Patricia Airways DC-3 crashed and the pilot, Dave Belluz, was killed. Three charges were laid against Patricia Airways under the federal Aeronautics Act that were later dropped in February, 1978, because the Crown prosecutor did not arrive in court on time. This is an incredible situation, but since then we have heard that the federal government is not going to proceed with
May 12, 1978

prosecuting Patricia Airways because the company has now declared bankruptcy. What possible relevance does the financial state of a company have in relation to compliance or non-compliance with the Aeronautics Act of Canada? If they have been violating the act, then people must be held responsible and appropriate charges laid. It is hogwash when the federal government uses the excuse of bankruptcy for non-prosecution.
The airline was charged with assigning Mr. Belluz to a plane when he had not passed an efficiency test on that type of aircraft within six months, as is required by law, with operating an aircraft that was not safe and fit, and with operating an aircraft in a sparsely settled area without the required emergency equipment. The inquest found that the plane had been overloaded by 500 pounds to 600 pounds, the logbook was not up to date, the entire history of the plane was sloppy and sporadic. The jury advised that maintenance be improved. It was also learned that sometimes officials concerned with the aircraft had been found intoxicated. Indeed, one of the employees had stated that she had been instructed to keep a logbook out of sight so that it did not fall into the wrong hands.
There is an example of one company which, it would appear, violated section after section of the act and which, it would appear, is responsible in no small way for the death of the pilot, yet we learn there will be no prosecution by the federal government. Mr. Speaker, when the House broke for lunch at 1 p.m. we were discussing the amendment placed on the order paper by my hon. friend from Vegreville. It would have the effect of amending Bill C-4 which is before us at the present time on the subject of the Aeronautics Act. The force of the amendment proposed by my hon. friend would be to ensure that when orders in council are made by the governor in council under the terms of this measure, the House of Commons would be able to scrutinize those orders to see that the government had acted properly within the power delegated to it by parliament. The amendment would provide for parliamentary review if 20 members signed a petition requesting it.
[Mr. Bcatty.l
I began earlier by noting that there had been an increasing tendency on the part of government to bypass parliament. What I should like to do this afternoon is to make four points. I think they are fundamental points. They are crucial, I believe, as we try to decide whether or not the amendment in the name of my hon. friend from Vegreville deserves support.
The first point I want to make is that the power of parliament is the power of the people of Canada. We have no rights except those which are drawn from the people. We act in their name upon authority delegated by them, and anything done to undermine the authority of parliament and lessen the power of the people's representatives undermines the power of the people themselves.
The second point I wish to make is that the government's increasing reliance upon the issuance of regulations is, in fact, undermining the authority of parliament. I will return to that point a little later.
The third is that the track record of the government with regard to government by regulation is bad, a dangerous one for the Canadian people.
The fourth and most important, I intend to establish that the amendment proposed by my hon. friend would give at least some protection to parliament and to the people.
I return for a few moments to the second point I made, namely, that the increasing reliance by the government upon governing by regulation is undermining parliament. 1 shall not deal this afternoon with other areas in which the government has been bypassing parliament or eroding its sovereignty by detracting from our ability to place a check upon the arbitrary powers of the cabinet, but it is worth mentioning that increasingly during this government's term of office the administration has relied upon orders in council, upon clauses in legislation which say that the governor in council "shall make regulations". A broad grant of powers having thus been given by parliament, the government is able, without returning to this House, to make decisions which affect the daily lives of Canadians.
I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a document which weighs about five pounds and contains over 1,000 pages. It is entitled "A Catalogue of Discretionary Powers in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970." This book, which simply lists the various discretionary powers held by the government-it does not elaborate on any of them-runs to more than 1,000 pages. What the government is proposing in the legislation now before us is to add to this list of the powers the government possesses to erode the freedom of Canadians without the consent or approval of the House of Commons. The government has increasingly been looking for ways in which to bypass parliament so that it can continue to rule Canada by order in council.
There was a book published several years ago entitled "The New Despotism," written by a former Lord Chief Justice of England, the Right Hon. Lord Hewart of Bury. Lord Hewart deals with means whereby a determined government could turn a parliamentary democracy into a despotism. I should like
May 12, 1978

to read a couple of passages from this book into the record because I believe they are germane to the subject we are considering.
Writers on the constitution have for a long time taught that its two leading features are the sovereignty from and the rule of law. To tamper with either of them was, it might be thought, a sufficiently serious undertaking. But how far more attractive to the ingenious and adventurous mind to deploy the one to defeat the other and to establish a despotism on the ruins of both! It is manifestly easy to point a superficial contrast between what was done or attempted in the days of our least wise kings and what is being done or attempted today. In those days the method was to defy parliament-and it failed. In these days the method is to cajole, to coerce and to use parliament-and it is strangely successful. The old despotism, which was defeated, offered parliament a challenge. The new despotism, which is not yet defeated, gives parliament an anaesthetic. The strategy is different but the goal is the same. It is to subordinate parliament, to evade the courts and to render the will, or the caprice of the executive unfettered and supreme.
That is the issue before us when we are faced with demands by the government for more power to allow it to rule by orders in council. I should like to put on the record also one further quotation from this book. It reads as follows:
It is one thing to confer power, subject to proper restrictions, to make regulations. It is another thing to give those regulations the force of a statute. It is one thing to make regulations which are to have no effect unless and until they are approved by parliament. It is another thing to make regulations behind the back of parliament which come into force without the assent or even the knowledge of parliament.
My third point was that the track record of this government with regard to governing by regulation is very bad. Nothing could be more germane when we are considering whether we should give the government the further discretionary power it is seeking. I will cite just one example. I would like to bring to the attention of the House today the report of the Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. That committee examined the government's use of orders in council as a means of avoiding coming back to parliament to increase postal rates. The committee made this short but very fundamental recommendation:
Your joint committee reaffirms its objection in principle to the use by the Crown of subordinate legislation under section 13 of the Financial Administration Act to prevail against parliament. It reiterates its grave doubts as to the validity of relying on the general power in section 13 of the Financial Administration Act to set postal rates, to override the special enactments contained in sections 10 and 11 of the Post Office Act, to overcome the will of parliament as to the domestic letter rate expressed subsequently to the enactment of section 13 of the Financial Administration Act, or to empower the Postmaster General to set rates when parliament has empowered neither the governor in council nor anyone else to do so.
The amendment which has been proposed by my colleague would refer orders in council which are made by the government under the terms of the amendments to the Aeronautics Act back to parliament so that interested members of parliament could have the authoritiy to examine the orders in council to see whether the government had acted properly.
It would also make provision for a committee of parliament to study those orders in council. On the basis of the way this government has operated in the past, we know that even when the appropriate committee of parliament has studied the abuse which has been made of orders in council by this government,
Aeronautics Act
the government has simply decided to ignore the recommendations which have been made by parliament. When the issue of the increase in the postal rates was raised in parliament, the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne), in response to a question in the House, made this one short statement:
I think we should put to ourselves the more serious question of trying to have more efficient delivery of mail everywhere, instead of wasting our time arguing if the rates are legal or not.
What more scathing indictment of this government could there be than the fact that the Postmaster General says he believes that parliament is wasting its time in questioning whether the government has acted legally or not? How can the government have the temerity to come back to parliament and say that it wants a vast grant of power which would be unchecked by parliament, when its track record shows that it does not deserve it?
All the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vegre-ville asks for is simply that in cases where it is clear to members of parliament that the government has gone too far in making an order in council or a regulation which is offensive to the Canadian people and of concern to parliament, parliament should have the right to review that regulation and to hold the government to account. I suggest that when this power has been given to this government in the past it has historically abused it, and it is clear that parliament must have some remedy to ensure that its rights and the sovereignty of the people of Canada are protected.
No issue is more fundamental to parliament than the rule of parliament itself, and I think that is why the proposal which is being made in this motion in the name of the hon. member for Vegreville deserves the support of every member in this House.
The one last point I would like to make is that the government denies that there is a need to have this parliamentary scrutiny of its actions by order in council. It says that what the government will be doing by order in council will be so innocuous that parliament would be wasting its time even to consider it.
Let me put the proposition another way. If in fact the regulations which will be passed by the government by order in council will be innocuous and of little concern to parliament, what cause does the government have to fear that parliamen-ta;y scrutiny would in any way endanger its ability to act? Unless the government has something to hide, and unless the government expects to be abusing the power it is asking parliament to give to it, it should have no objection whatsoever to allowing parliament to maintain its very fundamental right of keeping a check over the activities of the government. The proposal which is being made in this motion is eminently sensible. It is designed to protect the rights of the people of Canada, and I think it deserves the support of every single member of this House.

This bill is perhaps as good an example as any of the utter failure of the proper mechanical use of language. A piece of legislation is intended to be definitive in its object as it relates to the control of our society in one way or another. Because this legislation is not definitive or precise, it must lean on that crutch clause which appears in many bills in this House, the regulatory clause.
Regulatory clauses may sometimes include the phrase "notwithstanding any prior clause" or some other item which might be of consequence in the administration and intent of the particular bill involved. It is because of the practice of poor language that this government brings to us legislation requiring regulation to the extent that this and many other bills do. I am alarmed that this House, which has among its membership many outstanding barristers-most of them, of course, are on this side of the House, but the other side is also favoured with one or two-as the upholder of the law does not object in holy horror to the language of this bill and its transfer of power to the hands of an individual. This is the lazy man's way of presenting legislation. This legislation indicates improper consideration and lack of knowledge of its objective. It indicates lack of thought, lack of planning and, above all, bad government.
I am pleased that the regulatory clause of this bill has become a subject of debate because, while this principle may not relate specifically to aeronautics legislation, it relates to all legislation, and I think we must abandon the lazy man's way of planning the laws which regulate our society.
I suppose I would have to say that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has demonstrated to this House and to the country at large that he has a good command of the English language. His legal training and background should preclude the possibility that he, as a minister, would introduce legislation of this sloppy type. However, this legislation is not definitive or precise, and it is certainly not concise, and that should be the objective of all those who practise the mechanics of language.
In view of the fact the bill is sloppy and does not cover the field which will be later covered by regulation, I hope the government will indicate promptly that it will accept the amendment offered so that this House may consider the changes which may be made by regulation. Unfortunately, as pointed out by the last speaker, this is hidden law. I am going

to be repetetive. This is the kind of law which allows Canadians to go to bed innocent of any breach of legislation in our dominion, and wake up the next morning criminals. This is because the governor in council passed a regulation, behind closed doors, changing the rules of the game, as this bill will permit the governor in council to do.
When you think of a crutch you usually think of the maimed and unfortunates who are incapable of proper walking without some additional instrument to aid them. I submit that when a minister brings in an act which is as subject to regulation as this one is, which is as incomplete without regulation as this bill is, he is wearing a crutch. It indicates his incompetence by virtue of his use of the language in the bill which has been submitted for its purpose.
In the committee which sits on statutory instruments for this House, consideration is given to regulations which are passed by government. Although I may have missed something, it has not been drawn to my attention that government has accepted the fact that the statutory instruments committee has on occasion found fault with the regulations passed by government. In fact, on occasion I have found them reprehensible, neglectful, illegal and, worst of all, retroactive.
On one occasion when I participated in the deliberations of that committee, they were discussing a regulation passed to accommodate an error which had been made by the Canadian Feed Grains Board. The legislation spelled out very clearly some of the things they could do. However, having that basket clause at the bottom, it permitted them to circumvent the bill by virtue of regulation. They found they were in some conflict of certain aspects of their administration. They had to ask the governor in council to approve of an amendment which they had drafted and submitted to the proper minister who, in turn, submitted it to cabinet.
What that amendment did was legalize what could be properly classed as illegal behaviour by the board for a period of 15 to 18 months. That regulation was passed by cabinet and considered by the committee. To the best of my knowledge and belief, the government took no action to chastise or in any other way criticize the Canadian Feed Grains Board for their illegal behaviour. It patted them on the back, approved the regulation on a retroactive basis, and forgave them all of their sins.
That happened to be a relatively minor matter. Granted, the action which they took was probably positive as it related to the execution of their duties. However, it is an example of the incapacity of the draftsman to define the purpose of the act, and the crutch had to be used, a regulation. I want to emphasize the necessity of the House of Commons, with all the capabilities it has, having the opportunity to consider those regulations. It should have the opportunity to present them to the minister and receive his respect for the recommendations with regard to language. What we are talking about is incompetence in the use of language.
My early indoctrination into procedures of government in this country happened in the province of New Brunswick in the provincial legislature. I well remember about four people

Some of them have started as low down as the fisheries officer who, on his own, can virtually make a regulation. His superiors back him up after he has made a ruling. me, but I am quite sure that is the figure that appeared in a news release some time within the last year.
